metadata.description: A foundational network segment identifier — a VLAN (IEEE 802.1Q) or an overlay VNI (VXLAN/Geneve) — owned and advertised by a network/fabric provider and/or defined in a platform data layer, and SELECTED by reference from the resources that ride it (a Network.VirtualNetwork, a Hardware.NetworkInterface). A root resource (docs/guides/foundational-resources.md): dependents reference an existing VLAN, they do not invent one. The concrete encapsulation is provider data; a provider may offer a variant (e.g. Network.Port) that the org ratifies.

zone.description: WHAT KIND OF NETWORK THIS IS — DMZ, management, internal, storage — as a governed TAXONOMY term (Knowledge.TaxonomyTerm), not a property bundle and not a floor. A CLASSIFICATION, NOT A REQUIREMENT, and the distinction is why this is a taxonomy where `tier` is reference data: a floor is something a second provider can MEET, a category is something a thing IS. Taxonomy is also the only one of the two that carries `normalization_rules`, which is what this needs — providers report `dmz-2`, `DMZ_RESTRICTED` and `dmz restricted`, and all three have to land on one canonical term before any policy can match on it. FOR PLACEMENT ONLY (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Nothing critical hangs off a zone directly: it is not an authorization, not a control, and not a boundary. ANYTHING REQUIRED BECAUSE OF A ZONE IS ENFORCED BY POLICY READING IT — the model carries the classification, policy acts on it, which is the same split that governs everything else here. That also keeps the model on the right side of zero-trust architecture, which derives no trust from network location (NIST SP 800-207); UDLM already ships a `zero_trust.posture` setting that a location-as-trust reading would contradict. ON THE BASE though it does not apply to every network type (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10): enough of the family carries a category that the base is the right home, and an element that some types leave unpopulated is what `optional` is for. Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3) — a category two providers can both report is portable by definition. Provider-reported, like `tier`.

tier.description: HOW GOOD THIS NETWORK IS — a reference to a governed `network_tier`, exactly parallel to `storage_tier`. Each term DENOTES A FLOOR (bandwidth, latency), so asking for a tier is asking for the floor and any network meeting it qualifies: one provider's "10G" and another's "high-throughput" are interchangeable iff both clear it. That is what keeps the intent portable — the match is against the floor, never the string. NAME-SELECTABLE BUT REQUIREMENTS-AUTHORITATIVE (ADR-036, ruled 2026-07-27): a consumer may select by tier name, explicit requirements win where both are given, and the provider records its native class as a realized output rather than something the consumer had to know. ON THE BASE, NOT A TYPE, because performance is expected to be consumable by ALL network class providers and portable (maintainer ruling 2026-08-10). Scope IS portability (ADR-038 §3), so the category base is where a fact every provider must report belongs. Provider-reported at registration or discovery — the party that knows is the one that says.

encapsulation.description: Segmentation type. vlan = 802.1Q; vxlan/geneve = overlay VNI; flat = untagged.

segment_id.description: The VLAN id (1-4094 for 802.1Q) or VNI (0-16777215 for VXLAN/Geneve). Omitted for flat.

name.description: Human name for the segment, e.g. dmz.

segment_ready.description: Whether the segment is provisioned on the fabric and available to attach.

relationships.name: fabric
relationships.description: The switch(es)/fabric that carry this segment (where the provider manages it).

relationships.name: scope
relationships.description: Optional cluster/fabric scope the segment is defined within.

adopts.role: The overlay realization of the same segment identity 802.1Q gives on-prem — a VNI under VXLAN or Geneve. Adopted so `encapsulation` is honest about what this class actually is: a SEGMENT, of which a VLAN is one encapsulation.

adopts.version: AWS VPC / Azure VNet / GCP VPC (convergent de-facto model)
adopts.role: The public-cloud realization of segment identity. A cloud exposes no VLAN, so "which logical network" there is a subnet within a VPC, and `Network.Subnet` is where that lands. Adopted by reference (T5): the three clouds converged on the subnet shape independently, and re-expressing it would invent a fourth. THE VPC ITSELF HAS NO CLASS, stated rather than implied. VirtualNetwork is an ATTACHMENT POINT — its own description reads "the network a VM's or pod's NIC attaches to: a libvirt network, a NetworkAttachmentDefinition, an OVN logical switch". A VPC is a tenant-scoped CONTAINER with its own address space, holding many subnets, route tables and gateways. Treating one as the other would make a container and an attachment point the same thing, and a subnet is useful without its container — so the container half is left open rather than guessed at.

context.purpose: Names a network segment — an 802.1Q VLAN or an overlay VNI — once, as the shared object everything that rides it references.
context.plain_description: The segment itself: its `encapsulation` — spelled `vlan` for an 802.1Q tag, `vxlan` or `geneve` for an overlay VNI, `flat` for untagged — and its id, `segment_id`. It exists so a segment id appears in exactly one record — switch ports, host sub-interfaces, gateway segments, and virtual networks all reference the VLAN record rather than each retyping the tag. It is a root resource: dependents select an existing VLAN, they do not invent one inline.
use_when: You need one authoritative record per segment that ports, virtual networks, and gateway segments all reference.
You need overlay segments (VXLAN/Geneve VNIs) modeled with the same shape as 802.1Q VLANs.
not_for: The workload attachment point — Network.VirtualNetwork rides a VLAN; guests attach to the VirtualNetwork, not to the VLAN.
A port's tagging configuration — that is vlan_memberships on Hardware.NetworkInterface, referencing this record.
works_with: Hardware.NetworkInterface — ports and sub-interfaces declare membership by reference.
Network.VirtualNetwork — virtual networks ride a referenced segment.
Network.Switch — the fabric carrying the segment.
Network.Gateway — edge segments each ride a referenced VLAN.
